name: Heat protectant

lead: Heat protectants are sprays, serums and leave-ins applied before blow-drying or flat-ironing. They are marketed to reduce dryness, breakage and frizz from heat.
No clinical studies were found; claims rest on product and stylist descriptions.

paras: They are described as forming a film of silicones or polymers that slows heat reaching the hair, with water and conditioning agents spreading the heat and smoothing the cuticle.
No specific harms were identified in the reviewed material. Descriptions state the products reduce but do not eliminate damage, particularly at high temperatures.

lead: Heat protectants are hair-styling products, sold as sprays, serums and leave-in treatments, that are marketed to reduce thermal damage from blow dryers, flat irons and curling irons.[1] Descriptions say they coat the hair shaft with a film that slows heat transfer and limits moisture loss.[1]

Many products list protection up to about 450 degrees F (232 degrees C), and some also advertise conditioning or bond-repair ingredients.[1] Industry descriptions state that these products lessen but do not eliminate damage.[1]
No published clinical studies were found for heat protectants in the sources reviewed, so most statements about how well they work come from product descriptions and stylist recommendations.
infobox: Protection up to about 450 degrees F (232 degrees C)[1]
Silicones such as dimethicone, polymers, hydrolyzed proteins, oils[1]

paras: Products are applied to hair before heat styling. Descriptions list water-based formulas that absorb heat, silicone or polymer films that act as a physical barrier, and conditioning agents that smooth the cuticle.[1]
Newer products are described as combining heat shielding with repair claims, using peptides, bond-repairing complexes, plant proteins and oils.[1]

According to the reference text, heat removes bound water from hair, and heating wet hair rapidly can produce steam that cracks the cuticle. At higher temperatures, roughly above 180 to 200 degrees C, keratin proteins are described as denaturing.[1]
Heat protectants are described as emerging in the late twentieth century as heat styling tools became common. KMS Control, launched in 1984, is named as one of the first dedicated products.[1]

Product descriptions say heat protectants reduce breakage, frizz and dullness, and work best alongside lower heat settings.[1] These descriptions come from commercial and AI-generated summaries rather than controlled human trials, and independent measurement of the benefit was not found.

timeline.event: KMS Control is launched as an early dedicated heat-styling protection product (as described).[1]
